claim: VAT is the Thermoplasma acidophilum homologue of eukaryotic CDC48/p97.
source: VAT, the Thermoplasma acidophilum homologue of eukaryotic CDC48/p97, works in conjunction with the proteasome to degrade misfolded or damaged proteins.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract without supporting data in this manuscript, relying on established knowledge.

claim: VAT works in conjunction with the proteasome to degrade misfolded or damaged proteins.
source: VAT, the Thermoplasma acidophilum homologue of eukaryotic CDC48/p97, works in conjunction with the proteasome to degrade misfolded or damaged proteins.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge and supported by the experimental data showing VAT-dependent degradation with proteasome.

claim: In the presence of ATP, VAT with its regulatory N-terminal domains removed unfolds other VAT complexes as substrate.
source: We show that in the presence of ATP, VAT with its regulatory N-terminal domains removed unfolds other VAT complexes as substrate.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Substrate binding breaks the six-fold symmetry of the VAT complex.
source: Substrate binding breaks the six-fold symmetry of the complex, allowing five of the six VAT subunits to constrict into a tight helix that grips an ~80 Å stretch of unfolded protein.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure showing asymmetric substrate-bound conformation.

claim: Five of the six VAT subunits constrict into a tight helix that grips an ~80 Å stretch of unfolded protein.
source: Substrate binding breaks the six-fold symmetry of the complex, allowing five of the six VAT subunits to constrict into a tight helix that grips an ~80 Å stretch of unfolded protein.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure and measurements from the density map.

claim: The structure suggests a processive hand-over-hand unfolding mechanism where each VAT subunit releases the substrate in turn before re-engaging further along the target protein.
source: The structure suggests a processive hand-over-hand unfolding mechanism, where each VAT subunit releases the substrate in turn before re-engaging further along the target protein, thereby unfolding it.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and proposed as a mechanism based on the observed conformation.

claim: The 83 kDa VAT protein is composed of an N-terminal regulatory domain (NTD) and two tandem nucleotide-binding AAA+ domains (NBD1 and NBD2).
source: The 83 kDa VAT protein, which is composed of an N-terminal regulatory domain (NTD) and two tandem nucleotide-binding AAA+ domains (NBD1 and NBD2), assembles into a 500 kDa homohexamer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: VAT assembles into a 500 kDa homohexamer.
source: The 83 kDa VAT protein, which is composed of an N-terminal regulatory domain (NTD) and two tandem nucleotide-binding AAA+ domains (NBD1 and NBD2), assembles into a 500 kDa homohexamer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as known information and shown in the figure.

claim: Truncation of the first 182 residues of VAT removes the regulatory NTD, producing a construct (ΔN-VAT) that has both higher ATPase and unfoldase activity than the intact protein.
source: Truncation of the first 182 residues of VAT removes the regulatory NTD, producing a construct (ΔN-VAT) that has both higher ATPase and unfoldase activity than the intact protein (Gerega et al., 2005; Rothballer et al., 2007; Barthelme and Sauer, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In solutions of ΔN-VAT, the enzyme itself is degraded in an ATP- and proteasome-dependent manner.
source: In solutions of ΔN-VAT, the enzyme itself is degraded in an ATP- and proteasome-dependent manner (Figure 1a–c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1a-c.

claim: The 20S proteasome does not hydrolyze ATP during proteolysis.
source: The 20S proteasome does not hydrolyze ATP during proteolysis (Barthelme et al., 2014) and therefore this observation demonstrates that ΔN-VAT complexes must unfold other copies of ΔN-VAT via a process that requires ATP hydrolysis prior to degradation by the proteasome.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: ΔN-VAT complexes must unfold other copies of ΔN-VAT via a process that requires ATP hydrolysis prior to degradation by the proteasome.
source: The 20S proteasome does not hydrolyze ATP during proteolysis (Barthelme et al., 2014) and therefore this observation demonstrates that ΔN-VAT complexes must unfold other copies of ΔN-VAT via a process that requires ATP hydrolysis prior to degradation by the proteasome.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that degradation requires ATP and the knowledge that the proteasome doesn't hydrolyze ATP.

claim: VAT can recognize substrates with an unstructured N or C terminus.
source: VAT's ability to unfold pyruvate kinase (Figure 1b) and other VAT particles is consistent with the finding that it can recognize substrates with an unstructured N or C terminus (Gerega et al., 2005) and does not require a specific marker or target sequence for initiating protein unfolding.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: VAT does not require a specific marker or target sequence for initiating protein unfolding.
source: VAT's ability to unfold pyruvate kinase (Figure 1b) and other VAT particles is consistent with the finding that it can recognize substrates with an unstructured N or C terminus (Gerega et al., 2005) and does not require a specific marker or target sequence for initiating protein unfolding.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that VAT can unfold various substrates including itself, supported by citation.

claim: Cryo-EM of full-length VAT previously showed that the enzyme adopts a helical split-ring conformation in the presence of ADP.
source: Cryo-EM of full-length VAT previously showed that the enzyme adopts a helical split-ring conformation in the presence of ADP (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the same authors.

claim: ΔN-VAT particles with bound ADP assemble into long fibrils.
source: ΔN-VAT particles with bound ADP assemble into long fibrils (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is directly observed in the micrographs shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The fibrils are composed of helical split-ring structures interacting with each other top-to-bottom in a poorly-ordered helical filament.
source: Power spectra from these fibrils (e.g. Figure 1d, inset), as well as their real space appearance, suggest that they are composed of helical split-ring structures interacting with each other top-to-bottom in a poorly-ordered helical filament.
evidence: This is inferred from analysis of power spectra and visual appearance of the fibrils.

claim: The ~1/55 Å−1 distance from the origin to the first layer line is consistent with the pitch of each NBD helix in the split-ring structure of VAT.
source: The ~1/55 Å−1 distance from the origin to the first layer line is consistent with the pitch of each NBD helix in the split-ring structure of VAT.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of measured layer line spacing with the known structure.

claim: These fibrils were not observed in the ADP-bound state of full-length VAT, possibly because the NTDs block their formation due to steric hindrance.
source: These fibrils were not observed in the ADP-bound state of full-length VAT (Huang et al., 2016), possibly because the NTDs block their formation due to steric hindrance.
evidence: This is speculated based on the difference between full-length VAT and ΔN-VAT behavior, supported by citation.

claim: With ATPγS bound, full-length VAT exists in both the split-ring conformation and a six-fold symmetric stacked-ring conformation.
source: With the slowly-hydrolysable ATP-analogue ATPγS bound, full-length VAT exists in both the split-ring conformation and a six-fold symmetric stacked-ring conformation (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: ΔN-VAT with bound ATPγS forms a mixture of fibrils as well as single particles, the majority of which appeared to be six-fold symmetric.
source: Similarly, ΔN-VAT with bound ATPγS forms a mixture of fibrils (Figure 1e) as well as single particles, the majority of which appeared to be six-fold symmetric (Figure 1e, red circles).
evidence: This is directly observed in the micrographs shown in Figure 1e.

claim: A cryo-EM map of the six-fold symmetric stacked-ring conformation of VAT was calculated at 3.9 Å resolution.
source: This process allowed calculation of a cryo-EM map of the six-fold symmetric stacked-ring conformation of VAT at 3.9 Å resolution.
evidence: This is the reported resolution from the cryo-EM analysis.

claim: The 3.9 Å resolution is a substantial improvement over the 7.8 Å resolution obtained previously for the six-fold symmetric conformation of full length VAT.
source: This substantial improvement over the 7.8 Å resolution obtained previously for the six-fold symmetric conformation of full length VAT (Huang et al., 2016) is likely due to a number of factors.
evidence: This is stated by comparing the current resolution with a previously published resolution.

claim: Removal of the NTDs in ΔN-VAT makes the complex more structurally homogeneous.
source: First, removal of the NTDs in ΔN-VAT makes the complex more structurally homogeneous and allowed specimens to be prepared with thinner ice than could be used with full length VAT.
evidence: This is inferred as a reason for improved resolution.

claim: Specimen preparation with gold grids likely reduced beam-induced movement and improved image quality.
source: Specimen preparation with gold grids likely reduced beam-induced movement and improved image quality.
evidence: This is speculated as a contributing factor to improved resolution.

claim: Preparation of crowded specimens with ~700 particles per micrograph improved power spectra and allowed more accurate fitting of contrast transfer function parameters at high resolution.
source: Finally, preparation of crowded specimens with ~700 particles per micrograph improved power spectra and allowed more accurate fitting of contrast transfer function parameters at high resolution.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological improvement that contributed to better resolution.

claim: The map resolution enabled construction of an atomic model for the complex.
source: The map resolution enabled construction of an atomic model for the complex (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated and the model is shown in the figures.

claim: A central pore runs along the six-fold symmetry axis of the complex through the center of the stacked NBD1 and NBD2 rings.
source: In the structure, a central pore runs along the six-fold symmetry axis of the complex through the center of the stacked NBD1 and NBD2 rings (Figure 2a, left, hexagon).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Fourier shell correlation (FSC) of the map with the earlier map of full-length VAT with the NTDs excluded by masking reached 0.5 at 8 Å resolution.
source: While it is possible that removal of the NTDs affects the conformations of the NBDs, Fourier shell correlation (FSC) of the map with the earlier map of full-length VAT (Huang et al., 2016) with the NTDs excluded by masking reached 0.5 at 8 Å resolution, consistent with the 7.8 Å resolution of the full-length VAT map (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between the current and previous maps.

claim: The stacked-ring structure of VAT resembles recent structures of the VAT homologue p97 in the fully ATP-loaded state.
source: The stacked-ring structure of VAT resembles recent structures of the VAT homologue p97 in the fully ATP-loaded state (Zhang et al., 2000; DeLaBarre and Brunger, 2003; Banerjee et al., 2016), except for the orientations between the NBD1 and NBD2 domains in VAT protomers and the relative rotation of the NBD1 and NBD2 rings.
evidence: This is a comparison with previously published structures, supported by citations.

claim: All AAA+ unfoldases have conserved sequences that extend from the NBDs towards the center of the ring, forming 'pore loops' that are essential for unfolding substrate.
source: All AAA+ unfoldases have conserved sequences that extend from the NBDs towards the center of the ring, forming 'pore loops' that are essential for unfolding substrate (Gerega et al., 2005) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about AAA+ unfoldases, supported by citation.

claim: In the six-fold symmetric VAT structure, pore loop 1 of NBD1, containing conserved and essential tyrosine residues (Tyr264 and Tyr265), forms an opening that is ~28 Å across.
source: In the six-fold symmetric VAT structure, pore loop 1 of NBD1, containing conserved and essential tyrosine residues (Tyr264 and Tyr265) (Gerega et al., 2005), forms an opening that is ~28 Å across while pore loop 2 of NBD1 (residues 299 to 305) forms a slightly tighter aperture that is ~18 Å across (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, left).
evidence: This is measured from the structure and shown in the figure.

claim: Pore loop 2 of NBD1 (residues 299 to 305) forms a slightly tighter aperture that is ~18 Å across.
source: In the six-fold symmetric VAT structure, pore loop 1 of NBD1, containing conserved and essential tyrosine residues (Tyr264 and Tyr265) (Gerega et al., 2005), forms an opening that is ~28 Å across while pore loop 2 of NBD1 (residues 299 to 305) forms a slightly tighter aperture that is ~18 Å across (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, left).
evidence: This is measured from the structure and shown in the figure.

claim: Both NBD1 and NBD2 have strong density for ATPγS in their nucleotide-binding pockets.
source: An atomic model could be built for a significant fraction of the map (Figure 2b), including the linker region between NBD1 and NBD2 (Figure 2c, left), and both NBD1 and NBD2 have strong density for ATPγS in their nucleotide-binding pockets (Figure 2c, right) indicating that VAT adopts a rigid and symmetric conformation when fully loaded with nucleotide.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density map shown in Figure 2c.

claim: VAT adopts a rigid and symmetric conformation when fully loaded with nucleotide.
source: An atomic model could be built for a significant fraction of the map (Figure 2b), including the linker region between NBD1 and NBD2 (Figure 2c, left), and both NBD1 and NBD2 have strong density for ATPγS in their nucleotide-binding pockets (Figure 2c, right) indicating that VAT adopts a rigid and symmetric conformation when fully loaded with nucleotide.
evidence: This is inferred from the strong density for nucleotide and the quality of the map.

claim: Unsupervised classification of ATPγS-loaded ΔN-VAT particle images allowed identification of a second conformation of the protein that was significantly different from known structures.
source: Unsupervised classification of ATPγS-loaded ΔN-VAT particle images using a new ab initio 3D classification algorithm (Punjani et al., 2017) allowed identification of a second conformation of the protein that was significantly different from known structures.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the computational analysis.

claim: The class corresponding to the substrate-engaged conformation contained ~15% of particle images.
source: The class corresponding to this conformation, containing ~15% of particle images, showed two ΔN-VAT complexes in close apposition to one another (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is reported from the classification analysis.

claim: Refinement of the substrate-engaged structure achieved ~4.8 Å resolution.
source: Refinement of this structure to ~4.8 Å resolution revealed it to consist of a ΔN-VAT complex in the process of unfolding a neighboring complex as substrate (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is the reported resolution from the refinement.

claim: The substrate-engaged structure consists of a ΔN-VAT complex in the process of unfolding a neighboring complex as substrate.
source: Refinement of this structure to ~4.8 Å resolution revealed it to consist of a ΔN-VAT complex in the process of unfolding a neighboring complex as substrate (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is interpreted from the structure shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Formation of the substrate-engaged state may be dependent on the slow hydrolysis thought to occur with ATPγS.
source: Formation of this state may be dependent on the slow hydrolysis thought to occur with ATPγS.
evidence: This is speculated based on the conditions under which the state was observed.

claim: The map shows clear density for the substrate protein in an extended conformation as it runs almost directly through the central pore of the active ΔN-VAT.
source: The map shows clear density for the substrate protein in an extended conformation as it runs almost directly through the central pore of the active ΔN-VAT (Figure 3a and b, red density).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density map shown in Figure 3.

claim: The substrate-bound conformation displayed a strong preference for particles to lie with their long-axes parallel to the plane of the specimen support.
source: This substrate-bound conformation displayed a strong preference for particles to lie with their long-axes parallel to the plane of the specimen support, possibly because of the elongated shape of the complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is observed in the orientation distribution shown in the figure.

claim: Density for the substrate above NBD1 of the active ΔN-VAT complex is weak and fragmented.
source: Density for the substrate above NBD1 of the active ΔN-VAT complex is weak and fragmented, and is most clearly visualized without sharpening of the map (Figure 3a, above dashed line) (Zhao et al., 2015a), suggesting that outside of the active enzyme the substrate has a flexible orientation relative to the pore of ΔN-VAT.
evidence: This is observed in the density map and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Outside of the active enzyme the substrate has a flexible orientation relative to the pore of ΔN-VAT.
source: Density for the substrate above NBD1 of the active ΔN-VAT complex is weak and fragmented, and is most clearly visualized without sharpening of the map (Figure 3a, above dashed line) (Zhao et al., 2015a), suggesting that outside of the active enzyme the substrate has a flexible orientation relative to the pore of ΔN-VAT.
evidence: This is inferred from the weak and fragmented density.

claim: The length of unfolded protein gripped by the pore of the active ΔN-VAT is ~80 Å, which corresponds to 12 to 14 extended amino acid residues.
source: The length of unfolded protein gripped by the pore of the active ΔN-VAT is ~80 Å, which corresponds to 12 to 14 extended amino acid residues.
evidence: This is measured from the structure.

claim: In both NBD1 and NBD2 five of the six VAT subunits form close contacts with the substrate through their pore loops.
source: In both NBD1 and NBD2 five of the six VAT subunits form close contacts with the substrate through their pore loops (Figure 3b and c, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a and b, middle).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in the figures.

claim: The hydrophobic residues of the pore loops create a tight helical sheath around the substrate.
source: The hydrophobic residues of these pore loops create a tight helical sheath around the substrate (Figure 3a, green).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The top and bottom of the helix formed from the five subunits that grip the substrate are joined by a 'seam' subunit, which does not interact with the substrate.
source: The top and bottom of the helix formed from the five subunits that grip the substrate are joined by a 'seam' subunit, which does not interact with the substrate and has protomer-protomer contacts that differ dramatically from the other subunits (Figure 3c, gold, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a and b, middle).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in the figures.

claim: The seam subunit has protomer-protomer contacts that differ dramatically from the other subunits.
source: The top and bottom of the helix formed from the five subunits that grip the substrate are joined by a 'seam' subunit, which does not interact with the substrate and has protomer-protomer contacts that differ dramatically from the other subunits (Figure 3c, gold, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a and b, middle).
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: The helical arrangement of the pore loop residues maximizes the contact area between the unfolded substrate and the pore loops of the five subunits that form the helix.
source: This helical arrangement of the pore loop residues maximizes the contact area between the unfolded substrate and the pore loops of the five subunits that form the helix (Figure 3b, Video 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement shown in the figure.

claim: Unfolded substrate that spans the gap between the pore loops of NBD1 and NBD2 has a low density in the cryo-EM map, likely because of flexibility of the substrate in this region.
source: Unfolded substrate that spans the gap between the pore loops of NBD1 and NBD2 has a low density in the cryo-EM map, likely because of flexibility of the substrate in this region.
evidence: This is observed in the map and the flexibility is inferred as the reason.

claim: The flexibility of substrate between NBD1 and NBD2 is likely due to a lack of tension on the substrate in the observed state.
source: This flexibility is likely due to a lack of tension on the substrate in the observed state.
evidence: This is speculated as the reason for the observed flexibility.

claim: The transition from the stacked-ring to the substrate-engaged conformation of ΔN-VAT occurs with rearrangement of NBD1 relative to NBD2 in each protomer and a rotation of the NBD1 ring against the NBD2 ring.
source: The transition from the stacked-ring to the substrate-engaged conformation of ΔN-VAT occurs with rearrangement of NBD1 relative to NBD2 in each protomer and a rotation of the NBD1 ring against the NBD2 ring (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the two structures.

claim: In the substrate-bound state, the NDB1 and NBD2 of each protomer form similar interactions with their neighboring protomers.
source: In the resulting asymmetric structure, the NDB1 and NBD2 of each protomer form similar interactions with their neighboring protomers.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: The two rings are displaced horizontally relative to each other in the substrate-bound state and the central pore is tilted so that it passes between the rings at an angle of ~15°.
source: The two rings are also displaced horizontally relative to each other in the substrate-bound state and the central pore is tilted so that it passes between the rings at an angle of ~15° (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is measured from the structure shown in the figure.

claim: The rotation and displacement brings the NBD1 and NBD2 rings closer together than in the stacked-ring conformation, decreasing the distance between their pore loops.
source: This rotation and displacement brings the NBD1 and NBD2 rings closer together than in the stacked-ring conformation, decreasing the distance between their pore loops.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the two conformations.

claim: The six-fold symmetric stacked-ring state with ATPγS bound and the split-ring state with ADP bound likely correspond to pre- and post-unfolding conformations of the enzyme.
source: In this study, only the newly identified conformation described above is found with substrate bound. Consequently, the six-fold symmetric stacked-ring state with ATPγS bound and the split-ring state with ADP bound (Huang et al., 2016) likely correspond to pre- and post-unfolding conformations of the enzyme.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only the asymmetric state has substrate bound.

claim: In the substrate-bound conformation, the seam protomer is positioned such that it does not interact with the substrate.
source: In the substrate-bound conformation, the seam protomer is positioned such that it does not interact with the substrate.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: Recent structures of the 26S proteasome showed that either the Rpt5 or Rpt6 subunit in the hexameric Rpt ring of the 19S regulatory particle base is displaced from the pore, similar to the seam protomer in VAT.
source: Notably, recent structures of the 26S proteasome (Chen et al., 2016; Wehmer et al., 2017) also showed that either the Rpt5 or Rpt6 subunit in the hexameric Rpt ring of the 19S regulatory particle base is displaced from the pore, similar to the seam protomer in VAT (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a comparison with other published structures, supported by citations.

claim: The translocation mechanisms of AAA+ DNA helicases such as E1, Rho, and MCM involve a helical gripping state in which only five of six protomers interact with a single DNA strand.
source: Furthermore, the translocation mechanisms of AAA+ DNA helicases such as E1, Rho, and MCM, also involve a helical gripping state in which only five of six protomers interact with a single DNA strand (Lyubimov et al., 2011; Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012; Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as known information about other AAA+ enzymes, supported by citations.

claim: VAT operates processively with a 'hand-over-hand' mechanism where each protomer pulls a single section of the substrate, corresponding to ~13 Å or approximately two extended residues, through the central pore.
source: As the cycle continues, each protomer pulls a single section of the substrate, corresponding to ~13 Å or approximately two extended residues, through the central pore until it becomes the lowest protomer in the helix and releases the substrate (Video 3).
evidence: This is proposed based on the structure and illustrated in the video.

claim: The power stroke for substrate unfolding is provided by ATP hydrolysis, which occurs in sequence around the VAT ring.
source: The power stroke for substrate unfolding is provided by ATP hydrolysis, which occurs in sequence around the VAT ring, with ADP released by the protomer adjacent to the seam (counter clockwise from the seam when viewed from NBD1 toward NBD2, Figure 4b).
evidence: This is proposed as part of the mechanism based on the structure.

claim: ADP is released by the protomer adjacent to the seam (counter clockwise from the seam when viewed from NBD1 toward NBD2).
source: The power stroke for substrate unfolding is provided by ATP hydrolysis, which occurs in sequence around the VAT ring, with ADP released by the protomer adjacent to the seam (counter clockwise from the seam when viewed from NBD1 toward NBD2, Figure 4b).
evidence: This is proposed as part of the mechanism.

claim: ATP must rebind to the seam protomer as it engages with substrate at the top of the protomer helix.
source: Although the precise position where ATP hydrolysis and ADP release occur in the cycle is not apparent from our data, it is clear that ATP must rebind to the seam protomer as it engages with substrate at the top of the protomer helix.
evidence: This is inferred as a necessary step in the proposed mechanism.

claim: The cyclic nature of the ATP hydrolysis gives directionality to the substrate translocation.
source: The cyclic nature of the ATP hydrolysis gives directionality to the substrate translocation, allowing unfolded protein to be passed to the proteasome for degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the proposed mechanism.

claim: The cyclic 'hand-over-hand' model requires that each protomer hydrolyze ATP in turn.
source: The cyclic 'hand-over-hand' model requires that each protomer hydrolyze ATP in turn (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a logical requirement of the proposed model.

claim: A single inactivated subunit would have a severe effect on the rate of ATP hydrolysis, potentially stopping unfolding.
source: A single inactivated subunit would consequently have a severe effect on the rate of ATP hydrolysis, potentially stopping unfolding.
evidence: This is predicted from the proposed mechanism.

claim: A similar curve is obtained when measuring the unfolding rate of the ssRA tagged GFP substrate rather than the ATPase rate.
source: A similar curve is obtained when measuring the unfolding rate of the ssRA tagged GFP substrate rather than the ATPase rate (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: In the absence of an escape mechanism ATP hydrolysis would proceed from one protomer to the next in a cyclical manner until a defective subunit is reached, preventing further hydrolysis and substrate unfolding.
source: In the absence of an escape mechanism ATP hydrolysis would proceed from one protomer to the next in a cyclical manner (Figure 4b) until a defective subunit is reached, preventing further hydrolysis and, thus, subsequent substrate unfolding.
evidence: This is inferred as a consequence of the proposed mechanism without an escape pathway.

claim: If the machine is able to disengage at a stall point it would be possible for other functional subunits to hydrolyze ATP, although at reduced rates.
source: In contrast, if the machine is able to disengage at this point it would be possible for other functional subunits to hydrolyze ATP, although at reduced rates.
evidence: This is inferred as a consequence of an escape mechanism.

claim: The existence of an escape mechanism has important implications for substrate unfolding by allowing the release of stalled substrate.
source: The existence of an escape mechanism therefore has important implications for substrate unfolding, even in the context of wild type VAT, by allowing the release of stalled substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the proposed escape mechanism.

claim: Release of stalled substrate minimizes both the loss of active enzyme and increases catalytic efficiency.
source: This release minimizes both the loss of active enzyme and increases catalytic efficiency.
evidence: This is inferred as a benefit of the escape mechanism.

claim: Previous ATPase measurements with VAT followed Michaelis-Menten kinetics, with little cooperativity for ATP hydrolysis.
source: However, previous ATPase measurements with VAT followed Michaelis-Menten kinetics (Gerega et al., 2005), with little cooperativity for ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is stated based on a citation to previous work.

claim: Low cooperativity for ATP hydrolysis is inconsistent with simultaneous hydrolysis at all twelve nucleotide binding sites but is consistent with the proposed hand-over-hand mechanism.
source: This low cooperativity is inconsistent with simultaneous hydrolysis at all twelve nucleotide binding sites but is consistent with the proposed hand-over-hand mechanism, where only one NBD needs to bind and hydrolyze nucleotide at a time.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the kinetic data with the proposed mechanism.

claim: The sequential model for ATP hydrolysis is consistent with the asymmetry of the complex and nucleotide binding sites observed in the structure.
source: The sequential model for ATP hydrolysis is also consistent with the asymmetry of the complex and nucleotide binding sites observed here, and the homology between VAT and other AAA+ enzymes known to hydrolyze ATP in a sequential fashion (Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and comparison with other enzymes.

claim: ATP hydrolysis in the two NBDs has been shown to be coupled, with mutations in one domain also affecting ATP hydrolysis by the other.
source: ATP hydrolysis in the two NBDs has been shown to be coupled, with mutations in one domain also affecting ATP hydrolysis by the other (Gerega et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work.

claim: The mechanism proposed suggests that the two NBDs of each protomer move along the substrate in unison with each other.
source: The mechanism proposed here suggests that the two NBDs of each protomer move along the substrate in unison with each other (Figure 4a, Video 3).
evidence: This is proposed based on the structure and illustrated in the figure and video.

claim: Both NBD1 and NBD2 of each protomer form similar interactions with their neighboring protomers, and preserving these similar interactions would require that they function in concert with each other.
source: Both NBD1 and NBD2 of each protomer form similar interactions with their neighboring protomers. Preserving these similar interactions would require that they function in concert with each other.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: The conformations observed may be perturbed by the presence of the NTDs in full-length VAT.
source: These conformations may be perturbed by the presence of the NTDs in full-length VAT.
evidence: This is speculated as a potential difference between ΔN-VAT and full-length VAT.

claim: The conformations could differ when the enzyme is in a physiological mixture of ATP, ADP, and inorganic phosphate.
source: The conformations could also differ when the enzyme is in a physiological mixture of ATP, ADP, and inorganic phosphate, which could also affect the appearance of the bound substrate.
evidence: This is speculated as a potential limitation of the study conditions.

claim: The similar conformations of both NDB rings suggests that the mechanism of substrate unfolding proposed may operate in single-ring AAA+ unfoldases as well.
source: The similar conformations of both NDB rings suggests that the mechanism of substrate unfolding proposed here may well operate in single-ring AAA+ unfoldases as well, including Rpt1-6 of the 19S proteasome, and the hexameric PAN and ClpX unfoldases.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarity between the two rings and extended to other enzymes.

claim: AAA+ unfoldases adopt asymmetric substrate-bound conformations, creating narrow channels that sequester unfolded stretches of target proteins.
source: Thus, a picture emerges whereby AAA+ unfoldases adopt asymmetric substrate-bound conformations, creating narrow channels that sequester unfolded stretches of target proteins.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the structural observations.

claim: Even in molecular machines comprised of homo-oligomers, asymmetry can play an important functional role, in the case of VAT by priming the enzyme for processive translocation of its substrate.
source: Notably, even in molecular machines comprised of homo-oligomers, asymmetry can play an important functional role, in the case of VAT by priming the enzyme for processive translocation of its substrate.
evidence: This is a general conclusion about the functional importance of asymmetry, inferred from the VAT structure.

claim: Electron microscopy density maps are deposited in the Electron Microscopy Databank under accession codes EMD-8658 and EMD-8659.
source: Electron microscopy density maps are deposited in the Electron Microscopy Databank under accession codes EMD-8658 and EMD-8659.
evidence: This is stated as a data availability statement.

claim: Atomic models are deposited in the Protein Databank under accession codes 5VC7 and 5VCA.
source: Atomic models are deposited in the Protein Databank under accession codes 5VC7 and 5VCA.
evidence: This is stated as a data availability statement.

claim: VAT can unfold pyruvate kinase.
source: VAT's ability to unfold pyruvate kinase (Figure 1b) and other VAT particles is consistent with the finding that it can recognize substrates with an unstructured N or C terminus (Gerega et al., 2005) and does not require a specific marker or target sequence for initiating protein unfolding.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1b showing degradation of pyruvate kinase.

claim: Both ΔN-VAT and pyruvate kinase are degraded in an ATP and 20S proteasome dependent manner.
source: An SDS-PAGE gel showing that both ΔN-VAT and pyruvate kinase (part of the ATP regenerating system) are degraded in an ATP and 20S proteasome dependent manner.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1b.
